findings.title: A `d.run { ... }` block is not counted by blkMaxLevel, so the block arena array is one level too short: out-of-bounds `__extc_a[2]` write (ASan-verified stack buffer overflow), and a missing frame field in coroutines
findings.why: genStmtInner's ST_DOMAIN case (codegen.c:3778) emits the domain body with `genStmt(g, s->u.domain_.body)`, and that body is an ST_BLOCK (parser.c:2068), so genBlockBody increments `g->blkLevel` and every allocation/release inside the domain block uses one arena level deeper than the enclosing block. blkMaxLevel has no ST_DOMAIN case, so blkMaxOfBlock/`1 + blkMaxOfBlock(f->body)` undercounts by one. The count sizes the stack array `extc_arena __extc_a[maxLv + 1]` (codegen.c:4715/4758), so the emitted `extc_arena_release(&__extc_a[2])` / `extc_arena_alloc(&__extc_a[2], ...)` index one past the end of a 2-element array: `extc_arena_release` reads `a->top` out of bounds and, when it is garbage-non-NULL, walks and frees it (memory corruption). The same count sizes a coroutine frame's `arenaN` fields (check_top.c:6835) and `cgCoroArenaDestroy` (codegen.c:3403), so in a coroutine the generated C instead names a field that does not exist (`f->arena2`).
findings.trigger: Any allocation (or even just the block's release, when the function has an arena) inside a `d.run { ... }` block of a function whose enclosing body adds no other block level, e.g. `var buf: mut slice<u8> = new u8[4]` inside `d.run`. In a coroutine, any block-level `new` inside a `d.run` block makes the generated C uncompilable.
findings.repro: Program /tmp/rev/t_dom.extc: `use std::sys::domain` / `use std::io` / `fn main() -> i32 { let d = domain::single()  var tot: i64 = 0  d.run { var buf: mut slice<u8> = new u8[4]  buf[0] = 7  tot = tot + i64(buf[0]) }  io::cout << tot << "\n"  return 0 }`. `./build/extc /tmp/rev/t_dom.extc -o /tmp/rev/t_dom.c` succeeds (exit 0) and emits `extc_arena __extc_a[2]` plus three uses of `extc_arena_release(&__extc_a[2])`/`extc_arena_alloc(&__extc_a[2], ...)`. `gcc -std=c11 -O0 -fsanitize=address -o /tmp/rev/t_dom_asan /tmp/rev/t_dom.c && /tmp/rev/t_dom_asan` => `ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow ... READ of size 8 ... in extc_arena_release`, `'__extc_a' (line 814) <== Memory access at offset 160 overflows this variable`. Without ASan the same corruption is a plain SIGSEGV; /tmp/rev/t_domrecv2.extc segfaults in `extc_arena_release (&__extc_a[2])` (gdb frame #0/#1). Coroutine variant: /tmp/rev/t_corodom.extc emits `f->arena2` while the frame has only `arena1`; `./build/extc /tmp/rev/t_corodom.extc --check-c` => `error: 'struct co$frame' has no member named 'arena2'; did you mean 'arena1'?`. A plain nested `{ ... }` block emits `extc_arena __extc_a[3]` (size 3) - the contrast isolates the missing ST_DOMAIN case.

findings.title: String literals with `\xNN` followed by a hex-digit character are re-decoded by the C compiler under different rules: silently wrong bytes and length
findings.why: The lexer's own escape authority (src/lexer.c:336-372, `lexEscape`) consumes **at most two** hex digits for `\x` (comment: "`\xHH` takes one or two hex digits") and stores the token text verbatim, so at the extC level `"\x41B"` is the byte 0x41 followed by 'B'. EX_STR re-emits that raw text into a C literal, and C's `\x` consumes *unbounded* hex digits: `"\x41B"` is one character 0x41B truncated to 0x1B, and `sizeof("\x41B") - 1` is 1, not 2. The compiler therefore validates one escape syntax (it even rejects `\u64` for exactly this class of reason) and emits another; the mismatch is silent (gcc only warns `hex escape sequence out of range`), and both the bytes and the view's `.len` are wrong.
findings.trigger: Any string literal where a `\x` escape is immediately followed by a hex-digit character, e.g. `"\x00A"`, `"\x41B"`, or a binary-protocol literal such as `"\x1bE"` (E is a hex digit).

findings.title: cgLine evaluates an expression after flushPrefix (or without one), so the temporary it queues in the statement prefix is declared after the statement that reads it: generated C does not compile
findings.why: `genExpr`/`genBin` may call `pfLine`, which appends the temporary's declaration to the statement-prefix buffer; `flushPrefix` is the only thing that emits that buffer, and it must run *before* the line that uses the temporary. At 3756 (ST_TRAP, slice message) `genExpr(g, m)` is evaluated directly inside a cgLine with no flushPrefix at all (the same holds for the ref-message line at 3749-3751). At 4024 (compound assignment with a user-defined operator) `flushPrefix(g)` runs at 4016 and `genBin(g, s->u.assign.opExpr)` is evaluated *afterwards*, so its temporaries are queued post-flush. Either way the buffered declaration is flushed by the next statement and lands after its use, so the emitted C references an undeclared local. The checker accepts both programs; only `--check-c`/the C compiler notices.
findings.trigger: (a) `trap(<slice expr whose codegen needs a temp>)`, e.g. `trap(new u8[n()])` with an impure count (the checker marks the count needTemp, and EX_NEW emits `pfLine(g, "int64_t __extc_n%d = ...")`). (b) `x += <expr needing a temp>` where `+` is a user-defined operator, e.g. `a += (get() ?? vec2{ x: 2 })` with `get() -> option<vec2>` (EX_COALESCE with an impure subject emits `pfLine`).
findings.repro: (a) /tmp/rev/t_trap_new.extc: `fn n() -> i64 { return 3 }` / `fn main() -> i32 { trap(new u8[n()])  return 0 }`. `./build/extc /tmp/rev/t_trap_new.extc` exits 0 and emits `slice_u8 __extc_trap0 = { .data = ... (int64_t)(__extc_n1) ..., .len = (int64_t)(__extc_n1) }; fprintf(...); extc_die(1); int64_t __extc_n1 = (int64_t)(n());`. `./build/extc /tmp/rev/t_trap_new.extc --check-c` => `error: '__extc_n1' undeclared` + `extc: **the generated C does not compile** -- this is an extc bug, not a mistake in your program`. (b) /tmp/rev/t_pluseq.extc (struct vec2 with `fn +`, `a += (get() ?? vec2{ x: 2 })`) emits `a = vec2_add(&(a), &(((__extc_c1).tag == option_vec2_some ? ...` and only afterwards `option_vec2 __extc_c1 = get();`; `--check-c` fails the same way.

findings.title: blkMaxOfBlock evaluates blkMaxLevel twice per statement, making codegen exponential (2^nesting-depth) in the number of nested blocks: the compiler hangs on ~34 nested blocks
findings.why: The loop body calls blkMaxLevel on the same statement twice: once for the `>` test and again for the assignment. blkMaxLevel(ST_BLOCK) = 1 + blkMaxOfBlock(block), so each nested block branches into two identical recursive subtrees: with a chain of d nested blocks the cost is 2^d blkMaxLevel/blkMaxOfBlock calls. blkMaxOfBlock is called unconditionally for every function body in genFunc (codegen.c:4715 `int maxLv = 1 + blkMaxOfBlock(f->body);`), so this hits any function, allocating or not (confirmed: a checker error at the end of the deep body makes the compiler exit in 0.1s, i.e. the time is in codegen, and callgrind puts 45.91% in blkMaxOfBlock'2 + 43.39% in blkMaxLevel'2).
findings.trigger: One function whose body (or any nested block/if/while/match arm) nests blocks ~25 levels deep - e.g. machine-generated or fuzzed code. Depth 34 is effectively a hang; nothing bounds the depth.

findings.title: The receiver of a domain block is generated once per `ext` task and again for the run, so an impure receiver is evaluated N+1 times and the tasks are registered in a different domain than the one driven
findings.why: The receiver is kept as an ordinary `Expr` (`s->u.domain_.callee->u.field.obj`) and is printed wherever it is needed: for every task the EX_EXT case emits `extc_dom_add(%s, ...)` with `genExpr(g, e->extDom)` (codegen.c:2152), and here once more for `extc_dom_run`. An expression written once in the source is therefore evaluated 1+N times, in an order that also ignores source order (the body is generated before the receiver). With a side-effecting receiver the `ext` tasks are registered in freshly built domains while `extc_dom_run` drives yet another one, so the tasks silently never run. Neither the checker (check_stmt.c ST_DOMAIN only checks the receiver's type) nor the parser restricts the receiver to a place.
findings.trigger: A domain block whose receiver is not a plain place, e.g. `mk().run { ext task(i64(7)) }` or a method call returning a domain (`h.get().run { ext task(i64(7)) }`).
findings.repro: /tmp/rev/t_domrecv3.extc: a global `calls: i64`, `struct holder { d: domain }` with `fn get(self: ref holder) -> domain { calls = calls + 1  return self.d }`, and `fn main() -> i32 { var h: holder = holder{ d: domain::single() }  h.get().run { ext task(i64(7)) }  return i32(calls) }`. Emitted C contains `extc_dom_add(holder_get(&(h)), (void *)&__extc_dt0, task$domstep);` and later `extc_dom_run(holder_get(&(h)));` (two evaluations of one source expression). `gcc -std=c11 -O0 -o /tmp/rev/t_domrecv3 /tmp/rev/t_domrecv3.c && /tmp/rev/t_domrecv3; echo $?` prints `2`; expected `1` (the receiver is written once). With a receiver that builds a fresh domain per call (/tmp/rev/t_domrecv.extc: `mk().run { ext task(i64(7)) }`) the task is added to one domain and `extc_dom_run` drives a second, empty one. (Note: those two programs also sit on the P0 domain-arena bug, which is what makes the first variant segfault; t_domrecv3 exits normally with the wrong counter.)

findings.title: Negative-zero float literals are emitted as the integer `-0`, losing the sign: `1.0 / -0.0` prints `inf` instead of `-inf`
findings.code_quote:
if (isF32) return arenaPrintf(g->arena, "(float)%.9g", e->u.fval);
                return arenaPrintf(g->arena, "%.17g", e->u.fval);
findings.why: `%g`/`%.17g` never prints a `.` or exponent for an integral value (and drops the sign bit into a leading `-`), so `-0.0` is emitted as `-0`. In C that is the *integer* literal 0 under unary minus: the value is 0 and the sign bit is lost, so the double/f32 that reaches the program is +0.0. The float-ness has to be part of the spelling (`-0.0`), which the special-value branch above does for infinities but not for signed zero. IEEE-754 negative zero is observable through division, `copysign`, sign-sensitive branches and printing.
findings.trigger: Any expression whose literal value is a negative zero, e.g. `var z: f64 = -0.0` (or a negative-zero literal reached through a conversion such as `f32(-0.0)`).
findings.repro: /tmp/rev/t_negzero.extc: `use std::io` / `fn main() -> i32 { var z: f64 = -0.0  var w: f64 = 1.0  io::cout << (w / z) << "\n"  return 0 }`. Emitted C: `double z = (-0);`. `./build/extc /tmp/rev/t_negzero.extc --run` prints `inf`; expected `-inf` (IEEE-754, and what `w / -0.0` means in the language). gcc also warns `-Wfloat-conversion`-class nothing here, so the wrongness is silent.

findings.title: The EX_CALL handle-protocol block (next/value/send on a coroutine receiver) is unreachable, and its `send` argument index contradicts its own receiver selection - duplicated logic that has already diverged from genMethodCall
findings.why: Two things are wrong at once. (1) The guard needs `e->func != NULL` together with an EX_FIELD callee. The only producer of an EX_CALL with an EX_FIELD callee is the field-holding-`fn` rewrite (check_expr.c:3342 -> checkCallThroughFn, check_expr.c:1210), which sets `callViaFn` and leaves `e->func == NULL`; the checker rejects every other non-IDENT callee with "only direct calls to a function name are supported for now" (check_expr.c:2818). A gdb conditional breakpoint on this line (`break codegen.c:2327 if e->u.call.callee->kind == EX_FIELD`) over all 1871 .extc files in tests/, examples/ and bench/ fires only for callViaFn nodes and prints `func=(nil)` every time, and a breakpoint inside the block never fires - so the 35 lines (2327-2361) are dead. (2) If they ever became live, `send` would pass the wrong argument: `rf` treats `args[0]` as the receiver while the `vi` above treats `args[0]` as the value being sent, so `h.send(v)` would emit `extc_coro_send_T(h, h, ...)`. The live implementation in genMethodCall (codegen.c:1866-1888) takes the receiver from the node and the value from `u.method.args[0]`, i.e. the two copies already disagree.
findings.trigger: None today (dead code); it is a trap for anyone who changes the EX_CALL/EX_FIELD node shape, and it makes the comment at 2325-2331 ("a `ref coroutine<T>` receiver ... arrives here") false.
findings.repro:
No program shape reproduces it. Evidence: `printf 'set pagination off
break codegen.c:2327 if e->u.call.callee->kind == EX_FIELD
commands
silent
printf "FIELDCALL %%s %%d func=%%p\n", g->path, e->line, (void*)e->func
continue
end
run tests/coro/coro_handles.extc -o /tmp/out.c
quit
' > /tmp/rev/g.gdb; gdb -q -batch -x /tmp/rev/g.gdb ./build/extc` prints `func=(nil)` for every hit, while `while h.next() { s = s + h.value() }` and `h.send(i64(5))` on a `mut ref coroutine<i64>` are all resolved as EX_METHOD (genMethodCall) and emit correct calls.

findings.title: A lambda with no captures emits an empty initializer `(T){}`, which ISO C11 forbids and which leaves the synthesized `__extc_empty` field uninitialized
findings.why: With `e->u.lambda.inits.len == 0` the loop emits nothing and the result is `(<lambda struct>){}` - an empty initializer list, which C11 does not allow (it is a GNU extension/C23 feature; `-Wpedantic`, which this project uses for its own build, diagnoses it). The environment struct is deliberately given one field (`char __extc_empty;`), so the one field that exists is also left uninitialized. The first capture or a deliberate `{0}` would fix it; today the emission is only accidentally harmless because nothing reads that field.
findings.trigger: A lambda without captures: `var f = fn(x: i64) -> i64 { return x * i64(2) }`.
findings.repro: `./build/extc tests/lambda/no_capture.extc -o /tmp/rev/t_nocap.c` emits `$lam$main$0 f = ($lam$main$0){};` with `struct $lam$main$0 { char __extc_empty; };` (no field initializer). `gcc -std=c11 -Wpedantic -fsyntax-only /tmp/rev/t_nocap.c` => `warning: ISO C forbids empty initializer braces before C23 [-Wpedantic]`. The regression suite compiles the generated C without -Wpedantic, which is why it stays green.

coverage_notes: Read all of src/codegen.c 2151-4300 in chunks and re-read the dense parts: genExprInner (EX_ADD-DOM/EX_EXT tail, EX_LAMBDA, EX_INT/FLOAT/BOOL/STR, EX_IDENT with the coroutine-frame field rewrite and the hidden-arena fn-value rejection, EX_DEREF, EX_BIN, EX_UN, EX_FIELD, EX_CALL incl. domNew/viewOf/parWorker/coroutine-handle/boxed-coro/callViaFn/print/println/flush/name resolution/@overwrite-cell passing, EX_INDEX incl. array vs view and @unchecked, EX_ARRAYLIT, EX_SLICE, EX_TRY, EX_ASSOC, EX_CONV (int/float ranges and the i64 edge cases), EX_NEW, EX_GENCALL (alloc + all pool primitives + copyInto), EX_METHOD/EX_DYN/EX_STRUCTLIT, EX_REF, EX_COALESCE, EX_SIGN, EX_NULL, EX_ENUMVAL); genExpr's automatic deref wrapper; the ?-expansion helpers (TryInfo, tryPayloadPath, genTryFail, genTryHead incl. the main case); cgRecLeave/cgReturn; zoneArgRef/homeArg/arenaRefAt/arenaDriftCheck; blockMakesPool/cgReleaseLevel/cgCoroArenaDestroy; the @overwrite site walkers (collectOwSites/collectOwCallsExpr/collectOwCallsStmt) and owIndex/owCallIndex/owPassCells; blkMaxLevel/blkMaxOfBlock; genBlockBody and every genStmtInner case (TRAP, DOMAIN, VAR incl. coroutine spawn and @overwrite storage, ASSIGN, IF, WHILE, YIELD, RETURN, BREAK/CONTINUE, EXPR, BLOCK, MATCH); cgParamList. Checked and refuted (no finding): parWorker `nViews = params.len - 3` underflow and the `mutIdx` default (check_expr.c:3320-3345 requires >=4 params and exactly one mut view, and the arg count matches), cType(NULL) (returns "void"), EX_FIELD without subst (the checker rejects field access through a type parameter: "`T` is not a struct"), a user function named `print` (the checker intercepts it and reports a type error, not a silent miscompile), pool primitive arity incl. poolGive/copyInto (checkPoolPrim validates counts and types), @overwrite with a non-EX_NEW initializer (check_stmt.c:305 rejects it), EX_COALESCE with an array payload (compiles: arrays are structs in C, no decay), negative `new T[n]` lengths (extc_arena_alloc clamps to 1 and the view indexer traps on i<0 || i>=len), break/continue arena+zone release pairing (cgReleaseLevel uses the same zoneMark table genBlockBody writes, and loopLevel points at the loop body level), the char-literal path (it carries an integer, so the \x widening issue does not apply), and empty-capture lambda struct layout except as noted. Not covered: lines outside 2151-4300 (read only where needed for context: cgLine/pfLine/flushPrefix, cType, genFunc's prologue, genMethodCall's coroutine branches, the checker's ST_DOMAIN/parallel::run/@overwrite/trap checks).
